newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW - TUOMIOJA CALLS FOR MORE SOCIALIST POLICY.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - TUOMIOJA CALLS FOR MORE SOCIALIST POLICY.

text.p: Social Democratic Party (SDP) MPs think the government should adapt a more social democratic profile, Erkki Tuomioja, the new chairman of the SDP parliamentary group told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.

However, he also said that despite a left-wing setback in local and European Parliament elections last month, the group still firmly supports the government programme, including the effort to meet the criteria for European economic and monetary union, EMU.
"We are firmly behind this programme, there is simply no alternative," said Tuomioja, who was elected parliamentary group chairman on October 31, succeeding Pertti Paasio.

"But I would say there is a need for perhaps a stonger social democratic lable and presence in the government in general. Obviously we were concerned by the election results which went particularly against us," he said.
Tuomioja did not specify what he meant by a more social democratic lable, but said that calls for more of it was common feedback after the elections.

He explained the SDP's poor election performance by pointing to the low turnout -- unusually low in Finland at around 60 percent -- and said he did not think the voters were lost "but they must be motivated" to vote.

Tuomioja said SDP MPs are keeping an open mind about Finland's participation in EMU, and when the issue comes up in parliament -- likely in spring 1998, he said -- the vote should not be based on party discipline.

Tuomioja himself is known to prefer that EMU be postponed so that it could be improved and he again confirmed that view, but said his reservations about EMU pertained specifically to monetary union as it is laid down in the Maastrict Treaty.

"I have no opinion and I would not recommend anyone to have a strong opinion as yet on whether or not Finland should join the first group of countries in monetary union if economic and monetary union is created in the timetable foreseen."

He said the main problem is that EMU is not truly an economic union, only a monetary union, which has been driven strongly by people who believe it will then force further integration -- and economic convergence.
"That is not the right way to proceed," he said.
"You can't have a deeper federal union by stealth," he said, adding that it needed acceptance from all peoples participating.
He said he is not opposed to the government's effort to put the economy into shape for EMU.
"Even if there were no EMU, our economic policy would have to be geared in a way which would meet the criteria."

Despite that word of support, Tuomioja said Europe was suffering from unnecessarily high levels of unemployment because of the efforts to meet the criteria for EMU, as government budget slashing across the continent hits demand.

"You need to have flexibility. If there is a strong downturn in the economy, you cannot expect to reduce the deficits at the same time," he said, but emphasised that he was not advocating deficit spending, which he called a "dead end."
Tuomioja also saw scope for the Finnish government to do more to reduce unemployment.
"I think there is some scope for using, for example, shorter working hours, agreements on the sharing of work, more active labour market policies, and so on," he said.
"Anything which brings it down is for the good -- really down, I mean, and not just juggling the figures."

He did not have a view on the constitutional status of the EMU decision, i.e. on whether it should take a simple or a qualified majority to decide on joining and noted that in Finland, the constitutional committee is near free from party politics in deciding on proceedings in parliament.

In general, Tuomioja downplayed the differences in opinion between the Social Democrats in parliament and the government and said that the group's calls for new cabinet ministers was only normal in a situation where the government is expected to stay in office for the whole legislative term to 1999.

He declined to say whether a crack could emerge within the SDP if new spending cuts were needed, but said he expected forecasts to hold so that no new cuts would be required, though the government's 3.9 growth forecast looked optimistic.
"We would all want to see that (forecast) fulfilled, but it may be optimistic," Tuomioja said.
Acccording to Tuomioja, the drawbacks of EMU would not be remedied with the funds that Finnish unions demand as buffers to economic shocks, though he said he does support them.

"I do favour the funds because anything which increases the general stability of the economy and our ability to ride out recessions (...) is for the good, but I am not quite convinced that this has so much to do with the EMU problematics."
"EMU is good or bad regardless of funds," he said.
Tuomioja dodged the question of whether he sees eye-to-eye with Prime Minister Lipponen and said of the premier:
"He has an open mind, when he puts his mind to being open."
